hints.title: Use one angle for both sectors
hints.body: Sketch both sectors. Label the smaller radius r and their common angle θ radians.
hints.recap: Arc length is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> when the angle is in radians.
hints.pitfall: The curved edge is only part of a sector’s perimeter.
hints.pause: Use the smaller arc length to write an equation and make the angle its subject.

recall.reminder: Arc length is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>θ</mi></mrow></math> when the angle is in radians.

hints.title: Use the area difference
hints.body: Write the sector area for radius r and for radius r+3. Subtract them, then replace θ using your first equation.
hints.pause: Set the difference equal to 21 and solve for r.

hints.title: Include the straight edges
hints.body: Find the common angle. Each perimeter contains two radii and one arc; compare those parts separately.
hints.pitfall: Do not stop at the difference between the arc lengths.

solution:
Let the smaller radius be r and the common angle be θ radians. Its arc length gives rθ=6, so θ=6/r. The larger radius is r+3.

The area difference is 12((r+3)2−r2)θ=21. Substituting θ=6/r gives 18+27/r=21, hence r=9 and θ=2/3.

A sector perimeter is 2r+rθ. Therefore the larger perimeter exceeds the smaller by 2(3)+3θ=6+2=8. Answer C.
knowledgePattern: Common sector angle connects arc length, area and perimeter
